beats.speaker: Sifu, The Wise
beats.text:
Stop. Before you draw that blade, you will need a different weapon.

The thing waiting on this world cannot be cut. It can only be pinned down.

beats.speaker: Sifu, The Wise
beats.text: They call it the Ambiguous Client. It does not lie to you. It simply never says the same thing twice, and every version sounds reasonable when you hear it.

beats.title: A requirement is a claim you can check
beats.body:
A requirement states what the system must do, in language specific enough that someone can later prove it was done.

That last part is the whole discipline. "The system shall email a receipt after payment" can be tested. "The system should feel trustworthy" cannot — and a thing that cannot be tested cannot be delivered or disputed.

beats.title: Two kinds, and the difference matters
beats.left_body:
What the system does.

• The user can reset a password
• The admin can revoke access
• A receipt is sent after payment
beats.right_body:
How well it does it.

• Responds within 200ms
• Survives 1000 users at once
• Available 99.9% of the month

beats.title: The same request, twice
beats.good: “The dashboard renders in under 2 seconds for 95% of loads, and a new user completes their first report unaided in under 3 minutes.”
beats.verdict: Nothing was added. An opinion was turned into two things you can measure — and therefore two things you can argue about now, rather than after it is built.

beats.title: How a requirement is actually caught
steps: Elicit. Ask, watch people work, show them something wrong on purpose. They correct what they cannot describe.
Analyse. Find the contradictions between what two people told you. There are always some.
Specify. Write it down in language that can be checked, not admired.
Validate. Read it back to them. “Is this what you meant?” is the cheapest question in software.
Baseline. Agree it, date it, and treat every later change as a change — estimated and re-agreed, not absorbed.

beats.title: Requirements are gathered, not received
beats.body:
Stakeholders rarely state what they need. They state what they think they want, in the words of the job they already do.

A prototype is not a product — it is a question. Its value is the correction it provokes.

beats.question: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
options: The user can export their invoices as a PDF
The export completes within 5 seconds for a year of invoices
The user can filter invoices by date
An admin can delete an invoice
beats.explanation: Correct answer: the second. The other three say what the system does — functional. Only the time limit says how well it must do it. Note that it is still verifiable: a vague “exports should be quick” would be neither functional nor useful.

beats.title: Why the Client is dangerous
beats.body:
Requirements change. That is normal and not a failure.

What destroys projects is change that arrives unrecorded — a new expectation absorbed quietly, never re-estimated, never re-agreed. That is scope creep, and it does not announce itself. It arrives one reasonable sentence at a time.

beats.speaker: Sifu, The Wise
beats.text:
So when it contradicts itself — and it will — do not argue about which version is true.

Write both down. Make it choose. The written record is the only ground you will get to stand on.

beats.taunt: I'll know what I want when I see it. Show me something.
